topicName: Digital Forensics and Malware Analysis Basics
content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Digital Forensics and Malware Analysis Basics"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Digital forensics and malware analysis are foundational pillars of incident response and cyber security. When an organization suffers a breach, digital forensics focuses on preserving, identifying, extracting, and documenting computer evidence. Malware analysis runs in parallel to dissect malicious files, understand their capabilities, and develop detection signatures."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Phase 1: Digital Forensics Fundamentals"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"The primary objective of digital forensics is to maintain chain of custody and ensure data integrity. Investigators typically create bit-stream images of storage media rather than analyzing live systems directly to prevent altering metadata."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Volatile Memory (RAM): Captures running processes, network connections, and injected code before powering down the machine."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Non-Volatile Storage: Hard drives and solid-state drives containing the file system, registry hives, and deleted artifacts."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Network Artifacts: Firewall logs, proxy logs, and packet captures (PCAP) showing communication with command and control (C2) servers."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Phase 2: Introduction to Malware Analysis"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"Malware analysis is broken down into two distinct methodologies: static analysis and dynamic analysis. Analysts generally begin with static techniques before executing the code in a controlled, isolated environment."},{"order":10,"type":"subheading","text":"Static Analysis Techniques"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"Static analysis involves inspecting the binary without running it. This helps analysts quickly identify file types, embedded strings, hashes, and imported functions."},{"order":12,"type":"code","text":"strings suspicious_file.exe | grep -i \"http\""},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"The command above extracts ASCII and Unicode strings from the executable and filters for potential URL patterns, which may reveal C2 infrastructure."},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"Dynamic Analysis Techniques"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"Dynamic analysis requires executing the malware within a secure sandbox environment (such as Cuckoo Sandbox or an isolated virtual machine) to monitor its runtime behavior."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"File System Changes: Monitoring newly created, modified, or deleted files in sensitive directories like System32 or AppData."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Registry Modification: Tracking persistence mechanisms, such as keys added to \"Run\" or \"RunOnce\" in the Windows Registry."},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Network Activity: Observing DNS queries, outbound IP connections, and downloaded payloads."},{"order":19,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion and Best Practices"},{"order":20,"type":"paragraph","text":"Combining digital forensics with robust malware analysis allows security teams to rapidly scope incidents, eradicate threats, and implement defensive hardening. Always ensure that analysis takes place in an air-gapped laboratory to prevent accidental enterprise infection."}]
